strengths: The manuscript presents a coherent attempt to unify forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection using one pretrained architecture, combining autoregressive blank infilling with time-granularity-conditioned Fourier modules. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/89dc18edc72649efb309c13e6920571a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation spans several datasets and three practically important generative task families, with full per-horizon or per-mask-ratio results in the appendix.

The forecasting ablations consistently favor both the frequency module and time-granularity conditioning, while comparisons against random initialization provide evidence that pretraining offers modest benefits.
The architecture and pretraining objective are motivated clearly, and the paper provides useful high-level training specifications, dataset statistics, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: The central empirical premise is not established convincingly. Comparing frequency-amplitude densities from different datasets at different sampling rates confounds granularity with domain and data-generating process; moreover, different Nyquist ranges make visibly different distributions nearly inevitable. Controlled resampling experiments, normalized-frequency comparisons, and statistical tests are absent.

The Fourier mechanism is technically underspecified and potentially conceptually problematic. The stated 385-by-385 frequency matrices appear to arise from an FFT over the 768-dimensional learned feature axis, rather than over an explicitly defined temporal axis. The paper does not resolve the tensor dimensions, complex-valued parameterization, conjugate-symmetry requirements, or how the inverse FFT is guaranteed to return a valid real representation.

The experimental comparisons are not sufficiently controlled for a foundation-model claim. Most baseline numbers are cited from papers or source code under potentially different training, input-length, tuning, and pretraining conditions. Strong directly relevant foundation models discussed in the paper—such as Timer, TimesFM, MOIRAI, and Time-MoE—are largely absent from the downstream comparisons.

There are material result inconsistencies. For example, the main imputation table reports Weather PatchTST as 0.060/0.144 and Electricity Informer as 0.222/0.328, whereas the appendix reports 0.033/0.056 and 0.045/0.104, respectively. These errors change rankings and undermine the reliability of the claimed improvements. Other duplicated or inconsistent entries and averages are also present.

The claim of universal, task-agnostic adaptation is overstated. All downstream tasks involve fine-tuning, task-dependent preprocessing is changed, anomaly detection requires thresholding and point adjustment, and no zero-shot, few-shot, cross-granularity, or held-out-domain evaluation directly measures universal representation or transfer.

The anomaly-detection evaluation uses the controversial point-adjustment protocol, which can substantially inflate F1, without reporting unadjusted event- or point-level metrics, threshold-selection details, or comparisons to strong specialized anomaly detectors. Imputation likewise omits prominent specialized baselines.

The ablations cover only forecasting and do not isolate the blank-infilling objective against standard masked reconstruction or autoregressive pretraining. They also lack controls such as parameter-matched frequency layers, alternative granularity encodings, unseen granularities, and removal of the global frequency branch.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the claimed scale: no code or checkpoint availability is stated, and important details such as fine-tuning schedules, splits, masking-span distribution, forecasting input-length selection, anomaly thresholds, number of runs, random seeds, variance, parameter count, and computational cost are missing. No significance testing is reported.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: developing one pretrained time-series model for forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection. The manuscript and appendices provide broad experimental coverage across several public datasets. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/de5418a40abf4388bfafe5f0d4bc2d6c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Adapting autoregressive blank infilling to time-series patches is a reasonable design direction, and the shared projection layer offers a conceptually simple interface for multiple generative tasks.

The proposed low-rank, granularity-conditioned Fourier modules are computationally modest. Forecasting ablations consistently favor the full model over variants without frequency or granularity components.
The authors compare pretrained and randomly initialized versions and report full results for multiple horizons and missingness rates, rather than only selected aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: The central empirical premise is not convincingly established. Figures 1 and 3 compare different datasets and domains at different sampling rates using physical-frequency axes. Their spectra necessarily occupy different frequency ranges because the Nyquist frequency changes with sampling interval; dataset semantics, normalization, and signal characteristics are also confounded with granularity. There are no controlled resampling experiments on the same signals, statistical discrepancy tests, or evaluation on unseen granularities. Consequently, these plots do not demonstrate a novel intrinsic relationship or support the broad claim of learning universal representations.

The baseline comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Results are largely collected as the best numbers from papers or repositories under heterogeneous training, tuning, input-length, and preprocessing protocols—an issue the authors explicitly acknowledge. GTM additionally selects its lookback dynamically from 96 to 1440, without showing that baselines receive comparable context. This evidence cannot reliably support the claimed state-of-the-art superiority.

The claimed adaptation advantage is overstated. GTM is fine-tuned separately on downstream datasets, while preprocessing is changed by removing masking and 2D positional encoding and, for imputation, omitting patching. Thus the experiments do not demonstrate adaptation without task-specific intervention, zero-shot transfer, or a single model simultaneously solving the tasks.

The anomaly-detection evaluation relies exclusively on point-adjusted F1, which can substantially inflate performance, and does not specify a sufficiently reproducible threshold-selection protocol. No unadjusted F1, event-based measures, AUPRC, or threshold sensitivity is reported. Moreover, GTM is not best on several individual datasets, contrary to the surrounding language: DLinear and Informer outperform it on MSL, GPT4TS on SMD, and multiple methods on PSM.

Several numerical and narrative inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. For example, the five reported GTM anomaly scores average to about 87.16, whereas Table 4 reports 87.01 and Table 8 reports 87.15. In Table 13, the PatchTST Weather entries average to approximately 0.033 MSE and 0.056 MAE, not the reported 0.060 and 0.144. GTM is also not second-best on Electricity imputation according to the table, and Table 6 contains an extraneous forecasting-style Electricity row.

The ablations are inadequate for assigning gains to the proposed contributions. They are restricted to forecasting and do not compare blank infilling against standard masked reconstruction or autoregressive pretraining under matched architecture and compute. There are no controls for parameter count, the global Fourier branch, low-rank rank or module count, granularity encoding, incorrect/missing granularity metadata, or generalization to unseen sampling intervals. Results also lack multiple seeds, uncertainty, and significance tests.

The technical description is incomplete. The Fourier block does not clearly specify complex-valued parameterization, tensor dimensions, FFT normalization, or preservation of conjugate symmetry before the inverse FFT. The query construction and attention normalization are ambiguous, making the method difficult to reproduce or assess rigorously.

Reproducibility is limited despite some pretraining details: downstream optimizer schedules, epoch counts, early stopping and model-selection procedures, anomaly thresholds, random seeds, compute per task, parameter count, and code availability are missing. Overall, the idea is plausible, but the uncontrolled evaluation, unsupported central premise, and reporting errors are major issues rather than minor presentation problems.

The combination of time-granularity-conditioned Fourier modules and autoregressive blank-infilling pretraining is intuitive and potentially useful.
The evaluation covers several datasets, prediction horizons, missingness ratios, and three downstream task families.
The component and pretraining ablations consistently favor the complete model, while the forecasting results are generally competitive with the reported baselines.
The architecture, pretraining objective, dataset composition, and primary hyperparameters are described at a useful high level.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding is insufficiently established. Frequency distributions at different sampling rates are expected to differ, while the analysis compares heterogeneous datasets without controlling for domain, signal scale, normalization, or resampling the same process at multiple granularities. No quantitative statistical test or downstream cross-granularity experiment demonstrates that the observed differences constitute universal knowledge.

The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled for a top-tier foundation-model claim. Baseline numbers are selected from different papers or source code under potentially different preprocessing and tuning protocols, and major relevant foundation models discussed in the paper—such as Timer, MOIRAI, TimesFM, and Time-MoE—are absent from the main empirical comparisons.

There are consequential numerical inconsistencies. In Table 13, the Weather PatchTST average does not agree with its four rows; Weather and Electricity Informer averages appear swapped in Table 3; Electricity therefore does not achieve the claimed second-best imputation performance. The anomaly-detection average for GTM also differs between Tables 4 and 8, and Table 6 contains a duplicated forecasting row.

Claims of adaptation without modification are overstated: masking and positional encoding are removed, patching is omitted for imputation, and the model is fine-tuned separately. The paper does not evaluate zero-shot transfer or a single unchanged model across tasks.

The anomaly-detection protocol uses point adjustment, which can substantially inflate F1, but threshold selection and validation are not explained. Modern non-point-adjusted metrics and comparisons with dedicated recent anomaly detectors are missing.

The Fourier module is underspecified mathematically and operationally, including complex-valued transformations, tensor dimensions, softmax normalization, and how low-rank real-valued matrices act on FFT coefficients. This hinders assessment and reproduction.

Ablations are confined to forecasting and do not isolate the blank-infilling objective, masking choices, granularity encoding, parameter-count effects, or performance on unseen granularities. No variance over seeds or significance analysis is reported.

Reproducibility is limited by missing code or release information and incomplete downstream training, masking-span, tail-masking, early-stopping, and anomaly-threshold details. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evidence and internal consistency are not yet strong enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: developing a unified time-series foundation model that transfers across forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification.

The combination of granularity-conditioned frequency processing and hybrid reconstruction/forecasting pre-training is intuitively motivated and potentially useful, even though individual ingredients build substantially on prior Fourier modeling and GLM-style blank infilling.

The empirical scope is broad, including multiple downstream tasks, zero- and few-shot experiments, pre-training comparisons, recent forecasting baselines, anomaly-detection metrics, scalability studies, and efficiency measurements.

The forecasting results are generally competitive, and the authors provide repeated-run confidence intervals for several forecasting datasets. The extended TSB-AD evaluation is also preferable to relying exclusively on point-adjusted F1.
The appendix provides dataset statistics, major training hyperparameters, full per-horizon results, and some useful limitations.
weaknesses: The central Fourier-attention formulation is not technically well specified and appears dimensionally inconsistent. The paper defines H_FFT with shape N_total by D, but reports A_iB_i as a 385 by 385 matrix and left-multiplies it by H_FFT while using D=768. The FFT axis, complex-valued representation, tensor transformations, and dimensional reconciliation are not explained. This prevents verification of the main architectural contribution.

The evaluation contains serious internal inconsistencies. For Electricity imputation, Table 2 reports Informer as 0.222/0.328, whereas Table 22 reports 0.045/0.104; the latter would substantially outperform GTM's 0.086/0.202. PatchTST also outperforms GTM there, contradicting the statement that GTM is second best. The anomaly-detection average is reported as 87.01 in Table 3 but as 87.15 in Table 8. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the empirical conclusions.

Baseline comparability is insufficient. Many numbers are collected from papers or source code under potentially different look-back lengths, tuning budgets, pre-training data, and evaluation protocols, while GTM dynamically selects a look-back window between 96 and 1440. The authors explicitly acknowledge difficulty aligning settings but nevertheless make strong state-of-the-art claims. Classification is evaluated on only 10 selected UEA datasets without a clear selection rationale or uncertainty estimates.

The claimed task-agnostic adaptation is overstated. Different tasks remove masking, positional encoding, or patching; classification replaces the output head; anomaly detection requires thresholding and point adjustment. These may be reasonable adaptations, but they contradict the repeated claim of supporting generative tasks without task-specific modifications.

The proposed pre-training components are not adequately ablated. Experiments only remove frequency modeling or granularity conditioning; they do not isolate random masking, tail masking, span permutation, 2D positional encoding, the reconstruction objective, or the autoregressive objective. Consequently, the claimed benefit of the unified pre-training framework is not established.

The frequency-distribution analysis confounds sampling granularity with dataset/domain content. Comparing spectra from different datasets at different sampling rates does not show that granularity itself causes the observed differences; a controlled resampling experiment on the same underlying signals is needed.

Several broad claims are supported too weakly. Four pre-training data sizes and a small model grid do not establish a scaling law, and some measurements are non-monotonic. More concerningly, Table 30 reports exactly unchanged latency when look-back length grows from 1,440 to 14,400 and prediction length from 96 to 5,120, despite attention computation increasing with sequence length. Fourier attention also occupies roughly 0.033 of the reported 0.043 seconds, which is not a marginal overhead.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a foundation-model submission. The promised code link is blank, the exact UTSD constituent datasets and contamination audit are absent, and important fine-tuning details—splits, epochs, optimizer settings, model selection, threshold selection, number of seeds for most tasks, and preprocessing changes—are unspecified. The repeated-run means in Table 19 also do not exactly match the headline results.

Overall, the work has an interesting direction and substantial experimental breadth, but the malformed central specification, contradictory results, incomplete ablations, and non-unified comparisons are major issues rather than minor omissions. The evidence does not currently support the paper's strongest novelty, task-agnosticity, state-of-the-art, scalability, or efficiency claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a coherent combination of hybrid masked/autoregressive pre-training, temporal attention, and granularity-conditioned Fourier modules.

The empirical scope is broad, covering forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero/few-shot transfer, efficiency, and model/data scaling. The appendix also includes component ablations, repeated-run confidence intervals for some forecasting experiments, and stronger anomaly-detection metrics from TSB-AD.

Some results are promising: pre-training generally improves the same architecture, frequency-related components help consistently in the reported ablations, and GTM is competitive on several forecasting and anomaly-detection benchmarks.
weaknesses: The technical justification for the central Fourier contribution is unclear. The backbone representation has shape N_total by D, while the reported Fourier matrices have dimension 385, apparently corresponding to the rFFT of the 768-dimensional embedding. This suggests that the FFT operates over latent feature coordinates rather than physical time. Frequencies along an arbitrary learned embedding axis do not correspond to temporal frequencies, so the claimed connection to the amplitude/phase distributions in Figure 1 is unsupported. The FFT axis, tensor shapes, complex-valued operations, and residual/normalization structure are not specified adequately enough to resolve this concern.

The results contain serious internal inconsistencies. Most notably, the main imputation table reports Informer's Electricity result as 0.222/0.328 and identifies GTM as best, whereas the full appendix reports Informer at 0.045/0.104, substantially better than GTM's 0.086/0.202. The anomaly average is also reported as 87.01 in one table and approximately 87.15 elsewhere. Forecasting point estimates differ from the means used for the confidence-interval analysis, sometimes beyond the stated interval, without explanation. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the central empirical claims.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Many numbers are collected from papers or source code under potentially different preprocessing and tuning protocols, while GTM dynamically uses look-back windows as long as 1440; the paper's own sensitivity study shows that longer context materially improves performance. Comparisons against recent foundation models are incomplete, and Table 20 actually shows Time-MOE clearly outperforming GTM throughout ETTh1. Thus the claim of consistent state-of-the-art performance is overstated.

The advertised generative-task-agnostic adaptation is misleading. Forecasting removes masking, imputation removes patching, anomaly detection introduces thresholding and segment-level point adjustment, and classification replaces the output head. In particular, omitting patching appears dimensionally incompatible with the stated patch projection unless parameters or input layers are changed, but the implementation is not explained.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed pre-training ingredients: hybrid tail masking, span shuffling, two-dimensional positional encoding, and their interaction are never separately evaluated. Consequently, the claimed benefit of the novel unified objective is not established. Improvements from pre-training are also very small on several datasets.

The scaling-law claim is much stronger than the evidence. The paper presents a few mostly monotonic measurements after fine-tuning, without fitting a scaling relationship, controlling compute, reporting uncertainty, or separating increased data from increased optimization. This demonstrates limited scaling trends, not a scaling law.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a foundation-model submission: the promised code URL is blank, and important details such as seeds, fine-tuning schedules, validation/model-selection procedures, zero-shot protocol, anomaly thresholds, and preprocessing changes are missing or ambiguous. strengths: GTM combines a granularity-conditioned frequency-domain module with hybrid masked/autoregressive pre-training, offering a coherent approach to reusable time-series representations.
The empirical scope is broad: forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero-/few-shot transfer, pre-training comparisons, ablations, scaling, and efficiency are all considered.

Results are often competitive, including strong forecasting performance against recent foundation models, improvements from pre-training, and good results on the more rigorous TSB-AD anomaly benchmark.
The paper provides useful implementation information, full per-horizon results, confidence intervals for several forecasting datasets, and explicit analyses of model and data scaling.
weaknesses: The central claim of adaptation without task-specific modification is overstated. The paper removes masking and 2D positional encoding for forecasting, removes patching for imputation, replaces the output head for classification, and introduces anomaly-specific thresholding and point adjustment.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently controlled. Many results are taken from papers or code under potentially different look-back windows, tuning budgets, pre-training corpora, and evaluation settings; only a small subset of baselines is reproduced.

There are material reporting inconsistencies. For example, the appendix reports Informer at 0.045/0.104 on Electricity imputation, whereas the main table reports 0.222/0.328; the anomaly-detection average in Table 3 is also inconsistent with its constituent values and Table 8. These errors weaken confidence in the empirical conclusions.

The ablations do not isolate several claimed contributions—hybrid masking, span shuffling, 2D positional encoding, tail-masking probability, and the global frequency module—so the proposed pre-training framework is not adequately validated component by component.

The motivation for granularity-aware Fourier attention is confounded: Figure 1 compares different datasets/domains at different sampling rates, making it unclear whether the observed spectral differences arise from granularity rather than domain or signal content. Controlled resampling experiments are missing.

The Fourier-attention description is technically underspecified, with unclear FFT axes and dimensional compatibility between the stated 768-dimensional representations, 385-by-385 frequency operators, and Equation 3. Important backbone details such as residual paths, normalization, and feed-forward blocks are omitted.

The scaling-law claim is too strong for a few small, partly non-monotonic sweeps without fitted laws or compute-controlled comparisons. Likewise, exactly constant latency across order-of-magnitude increases in sequence lengths is insufficiently explained and difficult to reconcile with the architecture.

Reproducibility remains limited: the code link is blank, downstream optimization and model-selection details are sparse, and complete multi-seed uncertainty is not provided for most tasks. Overall, the ideas and breadth are promising, but the evidence is not yet reliable enough for acceptance at this threshold.
